extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary biography, literary critics, historians, and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing or evaluating literary biographies and critical lives: how biographers should handle facts, bias, motive-inference, and the relationship between an author's works and personal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid allowing enthusiasm to pervert judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The labour which has been bestowed on this volume has been a labour of love... but, on the other hand, we must frankly say that it has, to a great extent, perverted his judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enthusiasm for a subject can stimulate research but also bias conclusions. Reviewers/biographers should note where admiration leads to leniency, overlooked faults, or implausible rationalizations. Example/anti-pattern: praising a subject so strongly that inconvenient facts are reinterpreted to fit a flattering narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present facts openly; do not conceal or manipulate evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: He conceals nothing. He puts the facts before us in the full confidence that they will produce on our minds the effect which they have produced on his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A responsible biographer should make facts available and avoid trickery or suppression. If interpretation departs from the plain meaning of facts, the biographer should acknowledge that interpretive step. Anti-pattern: deliberate suppression or distortion of facts to produce a desired moral impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason from facts to motives; avoid inferring moral quality from assumed character
rubrics_metrics.description: To take a man's character for granted, and then from his character to infer the moral quality of all his actions, is surely a process the very reverse of that which is recommended in the Novum Organum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer motives only where evidence supports them; do not begin with a presumed character and retroactively explain every action. Prefer demonstration from documented acts and correspondence rather than speculative psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not idolize genius or make character a matter of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: The fanaticism of the devout worshipper of genius is proof against all evidence and all argument. The character of his idol is matter of faith; and the province of faith is not to be invaded by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should resist the temptation to excuse or whitewash moral failings because of literary greatness. Maintain rational evaluation even where the subject's works are beloved; separate aesthetic appreciation from moral assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply critical standards uniformly; avoid selective acuteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Middleton’s Life of Cicero is a striking instance of the influence of this sort of partiality... had the biographer brought to the examination of his favourite statesman but a very small part of the acuteness and severity which he displayed when he was engaged in investigating [others], he could not have failed to produce a most valuable history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same rigor and sceptical tools you apply to opponents when evaluating favourites. Inconsistency in standards (severe in some contexts, indulgent in others) undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disingenuous shifts, distortions, and suppressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resorted to the most disingenuous shifts, to unpardonable distortions and suppressions of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag and penalize rhetorical sleights-of-hand: selective quotation, misleading framing, omitted inconvenient episodes. Good biography acknowledges ambiguities and counter-evidence rather than disguising them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the value of works from the moral failings of the author
rubrics_metrics.description: A great writer is the friend and benefactor of his readers; and they cannot but judge of him under the deluding influence of friendship and gratitude... we forget the oppressor and the bigot in the historian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a subject's works may merit admiration while the person's private conduct may deserve censure. Critiques should explicate this distinction rather than collapsing aesthetic worth into personal virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about normative frameworks when evaluating institutions or policies
rubrics_metrics.description: We consider the primary end of Government as a purely temporal end, the protection of the persons and property of men... Government should be organised solely with a view to that end; and that no part of its efficiency for that end should be sacrificed in order to promote any other end however excellent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging institutions (or arguing about them), state the primary end or metric you use (e.g., protection of persons/property). Evaluate secondary aims only insofar as they affect the primary end. Example: assess whether patronage of the arts by the state sacrifices core governmental duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use power or authority to force secondary goods at the expense of primary ends
rubrics_metrics.description: All persecution directed against the persons or property of men is, on our principle, obviously indefensible... to secure the people from heresy by making their lives, their limbs, or their estates insecure, would be to sacrifice the primary end to the secondary end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political or moral argumentation, critique policies that employ coercion to achieve cultural/religious ends if they undermine core protections. As a critical principle, weigh harms to fundamental goods when considering secondary objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer effective means of instruction over doctrinal purity
rubrics_metrics.description: The only end of teaching is, that men may learn; and it is idle to talk of the duty of teaching truth in ways which only cause men to cling more firmly to falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating educational or proselytizing strategies (or analogous creative choices), prioritize approaches that actually convey understanding to the audience/context rather than insisting on an idealized form that provokes resistance. Example: choose the mode of presentation that will most likely educate the intended public.
